title: Transport of Deformable Vesicles Driven by Chiral Active Brownian Particles
abstract: Active matter systems can generate mechanical stresses that deform their surroundings, providing a route to transport and shape dynamics far from equilibrium. Deformable vesicles containing active particles offer a minimal setting in which such active stresses are directly coupled to boundary mechanics. Here, we use numerical simulations to investigate a two-dimensional, fixed-area vesicle filled with chiral active particles interacting through excluded volume and polar alignment. We find that the coupling between particle chirality and vesicle deformation produces distinct modes of collective motion, including run-and-tumble-like migration, rotor-like dynamics, and persistent spinning. Most notably, we show that vesicle rotation is non-monotonic in chirality: at fixed activity, an optimal chirality maximizes the rotational velocity. We develop an analytical theory that relates the vesicle rotation to the effective torque generated by the chiral active particles. The theory identifies the competition underlying the optimal chirality and predicts a scale-invariant dependence of the rotational velocity on activity and chirality. This scaling collapses simulation results obtained over different activity strengths onto a universal curve. Our results establish a general mechanism by which chirality and collective alignment regulate the transmission of active stresses to deformable boundaries, providing a framework for understanding transport and rotational dynamics in confined active systems.
summary: This work analyzes how chiral active particles drive the motion and shape changes of enclosed deformable vesicles. Using simulations and analytical theory, the authors show that chirality dictates the rotational dynamics, predicting an optimal chirality that maximizes rotation. This provides a general framework for understanding active stress transmission in confined, non-equilibrium systems.
main_problem: Investigating the transport and shape dynamics of deformable vesicles driven by chiral active Brownian particles (CABPs).
main_result: Vesicle rotation is non-monotonic with chirality, and the study establishes a general mechanism by which chirality and collective alignment regulate active stress transmission to deformable boundaries.
method: The study combines numerical simulations (Langevin dynamics) with the development of an analytical theory relating vesicle rotation to the effective torque generated by the active particles.
model_or_system: The system consists of a 2D, fixed-area vesicle filled with CABPs interacting via excluded volume and polar alignment. The vesicle is modeled as a bead-spring polymer ring, and particle dynamics are governed by Langevin equations.
key_observables: Mean-square displacement (MSD), asphericity ($\Delta$), and vesicle rotational velocity ($\Omega$).
important_parameters: Péclet number ($Pe$), dimensionless alignment strength ($g$), and chirality parameter ($\omega$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes fixed area conservation for the vesicle and focuses on 2D systems.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic models, simulation snapshots showing diverse vesicle shapes (rod-like, elliptical), and time-series profiles of observables like asphericity and MSD for different chiral regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the physical model and simulation setup to presenting simulation results characterizing distinct collective motion modes (Run-and-Tumble, Rotor, Spinner). It culminates in developing an analytical theory that predicts the non-monotonic dependence of rotation on chirality and deriving scaling laws.
why_interesting: The concepts of active stresses, non-equilibrium dynamics, and collective alignment are central to modern statistical mechanics, providing a concrete, solvable model for active matter physics.
